title: Can Viagra Advertising Make More Babies? Direct-to-Consumer Advertising on Public Health Outcomes
eligible_reason: Treatment is a continuous intensity (ED drug TV advertising dollars per 100 capita at DMA-month level), not a binary switch. Panel regressions of zip-month birth rate on ad intensity with zip and month fixed effects (and border-time, school-year fixed effects) are not a DiD with binary staggered adoption.
design_notes: Table 3 Models 1-5 (Massachusetts zip-month panel, 2001-2010): ED drug ads coefficient .008 (.003) in Model 1 (WLS, zip and month FE, N = 5,130), .007 (.003) with border-quarter FE, .007 (.003) with border-month FE, .007 (.003) with border-monthly FE, .008 (.003) with school-year FE (N = 4,940); SEs clustered by zip. The paper cites Shapiro's DMA-border design as 'akin to difference-in-differences' but the regressor is a continuous spending measure. The national birth certificate analysis (Table 5, 22,645 county-months) regresses imputed conceptions on log(1 + ED ad dollars per 100 capita) with county and month FE. No staggered binary adoption.
estimators_reported: WLS panel regressions with continuous ad intensity (Table 3)
county-month regressions on log(1 + ad dollars per 100 capita) with county and month FE (Table 5)
screener_notes: No replication package or regressions file was listed in the batch file (package_dir and regressions_path empty); screening is from the article text only. Advertising data are from Kantar Media (commercial), MA hospital birth records are restricted-access, and national birth certificate micro data (NVSS) are public-use. Not eligible under PROTOCOL Section 2 (continuous treatment intensity).
